title: Agent Builder's Playbook — Jul 31, 2026
intro: This edition centers on the boring-but-load-bearing stuff: a protocol spec you must not ignore, a benchmark that says stop trusting agents on oncall, and two ways to cut agent compute cost without touching the model.

cards.title: Update your MCP client and gateway for the stateless 2026-07-28 spec
cards.problem: The MCP 2026-07-28 spec dropped the initialize handshake and Mcp-Session-Id header, and remapped several JSON-RPC error codes to real HTTP status codes.
cards.apply: Stop relying on session state or persistent connections in your MCP client code — pass state through tool parameters instead. Update error handling for the changed codes (unknown method → HTTP 404, resource-not-found moved from -32002 to -32602, unsupported version → HTTP 400/-32022), and send the MCP-Protocol-Version header on every request since omitting it silently falls back to 2025-03-26. On your gateway, run one UpdateGateway call adding 2026-07-28 to supportedVersions alongside your existing versions.
cards.result: Servers stop needing sticky sessions and can scale horizontally behind a plain load balancer, while old and new clients keep working through the 12-month deprecation window.

evidence.note: Scaling and compatibility benefits are the editor's read of the documented protocol change, not a measured result.

cards.title: Try two-call self-refinement before reaching for a 5-agent pipeline on small models
cards.problem: Multi-agent pipelines are the default reach for hard reasoning tasks, but a 5-role pipeline can score below direct prompting on a local 7B model.
cards.apply: Before scaling to a multi-role agent pipeline on a local or small model, benchmark a plain two-call self-refine loop (generate, then critique-and-revise) against it on your exact task and output format — plaintext vs. JSON changed results more than agent count did.
cards.result: On GSM8K, two-call self-refinement beat a 5-agent pipeline (86.2% vs. 82% accuracy) at 7.4x fewer tokens; on HumanEval a naive version of the same idea dropped accuracy from 96.3% to 66.5%, so validate per task.

evidence.note: Accuracy and token-count figures are the paper's own benchmark measurements on GSM8K and HumanEval.

cards.title: Close the command-injection gap in your MCP tool handlers before adding a gateway
cards.problem: MCP tool handlers that build shell commands via string interpolation are exploitable through parameters the model controls, and a perimeter gateway alone doesn't stop it.
cards.apply: Replace string-interpolated exec()/eval()/subprocess.run(shell=True) calls in tool handlers with array-argument execution (e.g. execFile()), and add a CI gate (Semgrep rules) that blocks those unsafe patterns from merging. Pair it with an egress allow-list via NetworkPolicy so a compromised tool can't reach arbitrary outbound hosts.
cards.result: Closes the two cheapest attack paths — injected shell commands and unrestricted outbound calls — for close to zero runtime cost.

evidence.note: The article states the control cost as 'minimal' qualitatively; no measured before/after attack-rate figure is given.

cards.title: Don't trust an LLM agent's oncall root-cause diagnosis without a human gate
cards.problem: Agent builders assume frontier models can triage production incidents, but oncall root-cause analysis is a different skill than writing or patching code.
cards.apply: If you're piloting an LLM agent for oncall RCA, gate its output behind human review instead of auto-actioning it, and always give the agent source-code access alongside metrics/logs/traces — accuracy drops further without it. Benchmark it on a held-out set of past incidents with known ground truth before trusting it on live pages.
cards.result: On ORCA-bench's 1,079 real RCA tasks, even the strongest of five frontier agents scored 25.3% on medium-difficulty incidents and 10.0% on hard ones, and the weakest model hallucinated a root cause in 40% of reports.

evidence.note: Accuracy and hallucination-rate figures are ORCA-bench's own measured results across five tested frontier agents.

cards.title: Trim your agent's base harness prompt before optimizing anything else
cards.problem: A bloated base system prompt and always-on tool descriptions tax every single call an agent makes, even before it does any real work.
cards.apply: Audit your agent harness's static system prompt and always-on tool descriptions for redundant instructions, and cut them the way LangChain's Deep Agents v0.7 did — simplifying the base harness rather than layering on more scaffolding.
cards.result: LangChain reports 65% fewer base input tokens at comparable task performance after the harness simplification in Deep Agents v0.7.

evidence.note: The 65% figure is LangChain's own reported benchmark for the v0.7 release.

cards.title: Suspend idle agents instead of paying to keep them warm
cards.problem: Agent fleets that stay resident in dedicated microVMs burn compute while waiting on a human, a tool call, or a queue.
cards.apply: Move agent sandboxes off heavy microVMs onto lightweight gVisor-based sandboxes, then checkpoint idle agents to storage and resume them on-demand via an event gateway instead of leaving them running.
cards.result: Google reports this combination lifted agent density per node from 61 to 274 (4.5x) and cut cost per agent by 75%, with sub-5-second resume latency.

evidence.note: Density and cost-reduction figures are Google's own vendor-reported benchmark for GKE Agent Sandbox.
